first_impression.reaction: Sophie here. The intro describes our situation pretty much exactly: 'flights, villas, a venue, a photographer, guests arriving from three cities and deposits due in two currencies.' And I liked that it didn't oversell: 'None of that is out of reach on your own. It is simply slower.' That's honest, so I kept going. I skimmed the six benefits, then read the questions list properly because that's the part I'd actually use. James would read the takeaways and stop there.

journey.quote: A good advisor is one person keeping all of it in step, with quotes in Australian dollars and every inclusion confirmed in writing before you pay.
journey.reaction: AUD quotes and inclusions in writing are the two things that speak to my fear of hidden costs. Good opening promise.

journey.quote: None of these are shortcuts you are locked out of.
journey.reaction: I appreciate the honesty, but the headline says 'Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone' and then the article tells me I can get all of them alone. Small thing, but as a lawyer I notice when the heading and the body disagree.

journey.section: One point of contact from flights to the ceremony
journey.quote: If the ceremony moves by a day, one conversation should flow through to flights, room nights and supplier bookings, rather than six separate emails from you.
journey.reaction: That's the spreadsheet-at-night problem in one sentence. This is what I'd be paying for.

journey.quote: It turns a spreadsheet of euros, dollars and rupiah into one figure you can actually plan around.
journey.reaction: Yes. Mum and Dad are paying a big chunk, and they'll want one AUD number, not three currencies.

journey.section: Someone working in your time zone
journey.quote: Planning a wedding in Europe from Sydney or Perth means waking to replies sent at midnight your time, and answering them before the other side has gone to bed.
journey.reaction: Very real. I already do this for work with London and I don't want to do it for the wedding too.

journey.section: Your consumer rights, booked either way
journey.quote: Booking through an advisor does not give you stronger rights, and it does not take any away.
journey.reaction: Honest and correct, but it's listed as one of the 'six ways an advisor makes a wedding trip easier' when it's really a disclaimer. And this consumer-guarantee point has now come up three times. It starts to feel like a government fact sheet rather than someone who has actually run a wedding week.

journey.section: What you can book yourself, and where it gets harder
journey.quote: Arrival dates, room allocations, dietary notes and the cousin who changes flights twice.
journey.reaction: Ha, we have that cousin. This is the most human line on the page. It makes me think about Grandma too.

journey.section: What you can book yourself, and where it gets harder
journey.quote: If most of those answers are "me", in the months before your wedding, that is the work an advisor takes on.
journey.reaction: Good self-check. Most of the answers are 'me', which is the point. But nowhere does it get into the thing I worry about most, older guests getting from the airport to the venue. It mentions 'transport between them' once and moves on.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: Do you hold insolvency insurance? Travel provider or agent insolvency is commonly excluded from cancellation cover, and only a few insurers cover it.
journey.reaction: I hadn't thought about this at all and it's exactly the 'no one accountable' fear. This list is the most useful part of the page. I'd forward it to Dad.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: These apply to any advisor, whoever you speak with. Ask them early, and ask for the answers in writing.
journey.reaction: Fair and not salesy. Though the obvious next thought is: so what are Wedded Wonderland's answers? The page gives me eight questions and only really answers the fee-in-writing one for itself.

journey.section: When the trip is a wedding and a honeymoon
journey.quote: It helps to plan both halves at once. The wedding fixes the dates and the first base.
journey.reaction: Sensible, and we hadn't really linked the two yet. A one-line example (say, Greece wedding then where?) would have made it feel lived-in rather than general.

journey.section: When the trip is a wedding and a honeymoon
journey.quote: With Wedded Concierge, one Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD.
journey.reaction: Clear and not pushy. 'Single point of contact' is the thing I want. Every planner says end-to-end though, so I'd still want to know what that means on the actual wedding day.

unanswered_questions: How is the Wedded Concierge fee charged (flat, percentage, commission), and roughly how much? The page says it's agreed in writing but not what it's based on.
On the wedding day itself, is the Wedded Advisor or someone from the team physically there, or are local suppliers left to run it?
Do you hold insolvency insurance and belong to an accreditation scheme, given the article tells me to ask?
Who handles guest airport transfers and room blocks for 60 to 90 guests, including older relatives?
Is there a real wedding (venue and date) where you planned both the wedding week and the honeymoon for an Australian couple?
Are there any extras or perks from booking through you rather than direct?
would_share_with: Mum and Dad, since they're contributing: the eight questions to ask before hiring an advisor, especially insolvency insurance and credit card payment

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like to talk through your wedding and honeymoon, [speak with Wedded Concierge]
cta_reaction.why: It's low-pressure and the fee-in-writing line before it helps. But this is a general 'why use an advisor' article, and I still haven't seen a real wedding or how the fee works. I'd bookmark it, read a destination post and look for a real wedding first. I'd click the Greece link before the enquiry link.

top_3_changes: Add one concrete, wedding-specific scenario (for example guests, including older relatives, flying in from three cities and getting from the airport to the venue) so it reads like someone who has run a wedding week, not a general travel guide. It's the insider detail that earns my trust.

Trim the repeated consumer-guarantee point (it appears in the 'what does an advisor do' section, as benefit six and in the FAQ) and reframe benefit six as 'an advisor walks you through both sets of terms', so the six benefits all read as benefits.
Line the headline up with the body: the article honestly says nothing is out of reach booking alone, so 'Cannot Get Booking Alone' feels like a slight overclaim next to it.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Sophie & James (Sydney, early research, 14 months out, no spreadsheets, guests and grandparents)
No invented brand facts; anything the page doesn't say is listed in unanswered_questions
[[VERIFY]] markers and HTML comments ignored as invisible
Didn't invent problems; positives recorded where the draft earns them; no turn-offs found
Business-deferred details (fee basis, commissions, on-the-ground presence, scale proof, perks, Wedded Privileges) kept to unanswered_questions, not top_3_changes

assumptions: Persona is provisional (not CRM-calibrated), so these reactions reflect the assumed profile.
Fee basis, on-the-ground presence, real-wedding proof and perks are deferred by the business, so they appear only as unanswered questions.
